title: True Genius Expresses Itself in Multiple Mediums
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using Picasso, Bob Dylan, and Paul Newman as examples, this piece argues that the defining trait separating genius from mere high talent is the ability to apply the same underlying creative insight across multiple, unrelated disciplines. The author cites biographer Walter Isaacson's view that this cross-domain application of imaginative thinking — not raw intelligence — is what distinguishes truly exceptional individuals. The piece closes with a call to try one's own hand at multiple mediums as a way of expressing latent creative capacity.
points: The defining trait of genius, as opposed to high talent, is the ability to apply the same underlying insight across multiple, unrelated disciplines.
Examples cited include Picasso across painting, sculpture, printmaking, and ceramics, and Paul Newman across acting, directing, racing, and cooking.
Biographer Walter Isaacson's research on figures like da Vinci and Franklin found imaginative, cross-domain thinking as the most common trait among true geniuses.
The distinction between talent and genius is framed via Schopenhauer: talent hits a target no one else can hit, genius hits a target no one else can see.
quotes: Picasso wasn’t just a world-class painter. He was also a master sculptor, a consummate printmaker, a celebrated ceramicist, and an innovative theatre designer.
Genius can’t help but express itself in multiple disciplines. That’s how to distinguish genius from high talent.
Talent hits a target no one else can hit; genius hits a target no one else can see.
The most common trait shared by these extraordinary individuals is their ability to apply creativity and imaginative thinking to almost any situation.
Smart people are a dime a dozen. What matters is the ability to think differently, to think out of the box.
